summary: Markets are trading in a distinctly risk-off mood as escalating U.S.-Iran military conflict dominates sentiment, with Brent crude surging past $100 per barrel for the first time in years after Houthi attacks on Saudi cities, an oil tanker struck in Iraqi waters, and the EIA hiking its oil price forecasts citing draining global stockpiles. On the macro front, the U.S. Treasury announced a $6 billion buyback operation scheduled for September 10, while geopolitical friction expanded with Pakistan warning Iran to restrain the Houthis, Turkey acknowledging U.S.-Iran sanctions implications, and the UAE and Germany pursuing investment and energy deals that signal realignment around supply security. Energy stocks are outperforming broadly as the Iran war premium embeds into crude prices, while Dow Chemical faces pressure on reports it may exit its $20 billion Aramco partnership, GE Aerospace is drawing attention for supply chain investments in jet engine castings, and data center stocks remain under scrutiny with Cramer advising caution amid valuation concerns. The primary risk factors investors are monitoring include a further escalation of the U.S.-Iran conflict disrupting global oil supply routes, secondary sanctions contagion affecting Turkey and other emerging markets, the ongoing federal criminal trial against Huawei potentially straining U.S.-China trade relations, and political uncertainty in Washington as Republicans begin debating a post-Trump future. In the short term, elevated oil prices are likely to sustain energy sector outperformance while pressuring consumer and industrial margins, and markets will remain highly sensitive to any de-escalation signals from the Middle East, with Trump's comment that the Iran war will end after U.S. midterm elections introducing a specific but uncertain timeline traders will closely watch.
